title: The Day Reversed and the Feast of Purim
summary: On the thirteenth of Adar, the day Haman had chosen for their destruction, the Jews overpower their enemies across the empire, killing Haman's ten sons and many who hated them, but taking no plunder. At Esther's request the fighting in Susa continues a second day. The Jews rest and celebrate, and Mordecai and Esther write letters establishing the annual feast of Purim, named for the lot Haman cast.
story: Chapter 8 ended with the second decree sent out and the Jews celebrating in advance. Here the day arrives. The book has been moving toward this date since Haman cast the lot in chapter 3, and now the plan is overturned. The second half of the chapter shifts from narrative to explanation: it tells why the festival of Purim is kept, why it falls on two different days, and what it involves. This is the purpose the whole book serves. Esther is, among other things, the story behind a festival that Jews have kept ever since, and this chapter makes that connection explicit.
historical:
The events take place on the thirteenth and fourteenth of Adar, the twelfth month of the year (late winter), in about 473 BC, eleven months after Haman's decree was issued. The officials who help the Jews, satraps, governors, and royal administrators, act out of fear of Mordecai, now the empire's second-ranking official. The Greek translation of Esther gives a smaller figure than the Hebrew for those killed in the provinces (15,000 instead of 75,000), one of several places where the ancient versions differ.

The festival of Purim is attested outside the book by the second century BC. Second Maccabees, in the Apocrypha, refers to the fourteenth of Adar as Mordecai's day, showing that the celebration was known in Judea by then. Purim was not one of the festivals commanded in the law of Moses; it was established by the Jewish community itself and accepted as binding, as this chapter describes.
cultural:
The word Pur comes from the Akkadian word puru, meaning a lot, a small object cast to reach a decision. Haman used it to choose the day for the destruction of the Jews, trusting in fate or the gods to give him a favorable day. The festival takes its name, Purim (the plural), from that lot, a pointed reminder that the day chosen for Israel's destruction became the day of its deliverance.

The chapter explains a difference that is still observed. Jews in the villages celebrate on the fourteenth of Adar, while in Susa the fighting continued a second day, so the celebration there was on the fifteenth. Later Jewish practice kept both: most communities celebrate on the fourteenth, and cities that were walled in the time of Joshua, above all Jerusalem, celebrate on the fifteenth, called Shushan Purim after Susa. The customs named in verse 22 remain central to the festival to this day: feasting and joy, sending portions of food to one another, and gifts to the poor. The public reading of the scroll of Esther, often with noise to drown out Haman's name, developed later in Jewish tradition.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-19 narrate the fighting and the rest that follows, repeating that the Jews did not lay a hand on the plunder three times (verses 10, 15, 16). Verse 1 states the book's great theme in a single word: the situation was overturned, so that those who hoped to master the Jews were mastered by them. Verses 20-32 read almost like an official record, with the letters of Mordecai and Esther and the regulations for the feast, repeating the words days, joy, feasting, and remembrance. The list of Haman's ten sons in verses 7-9 is set out in the Hebrew scroll in a distinctive column arrangement, which marks it visually. The summary in verses 24-25 retells the whole story in a few lines, emphasizing that Haman's scheme returned on his own head.

outline.t: The day is overturned and officials help the Jews
Fighting in Susa and the death of Haman's sons
A second day in Susa at Esther's request
Victory in the provinces and days of rest and feasting
Mordecai establishes the annual feast of Purim
Esther confirms the regulations for Purim

doctrines.note: Haman trusted the lot to choose the day of destruction, but the day became one of deliverance. Proverbs 16:33 expresses the conviction behind this: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

The enemies of the Jews fall on the day they meant to destroy them, and Haman's sons share his end. The chapter presents their defeat as the just return of their own violence, not as unprovoked aggression.
The festival turns sorrow into joy and mourning into celebration. Purim teaches God's people to remember past deliverance as grounds for hope in future danger.

words.note: Haphakh, to turn or overturn. Verse 1 says that the plan was overturned, and the same verb describes sorrow turned to joy in verse 22. It is the key word of the whole book: nearly every element of Haman's plot is reversed against him.

Pur, lot. A loanword from Akkadian, explained in verse 24 as the lot. The feast of Purim takes its name from the lot Haman cast to choose the day, a reminder that the enemy's chosen day of destruction became the day of rescue.

Bizzah, plunder or spoil. Three times the text says the Jews took no plunder, even though the decree allowed it (8:11). Many interpreters connect this with Saul's failure in 1 Samuel 15, when he took the best of the plunder from the Amalekites and spared Agag, the king whose name Haman's title Agagite recalls.

Zakhar, to remember. These days are to be remembered and kept in every generation. Remembrance in the Old Testament is active: it means rehearsing and celebrating what God has done so that each new generation takes part in it.

christ: The Bible repeatedly tells of God turning the day of his people's destruction into a day of rescue, and this chapter is one of the clearest examples. The ultimate reversal, in the Christian reading, is the cross and resurrection, where the day of Jesus' death became the day of salvation. Jesus told his disciples, “You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy” (John 16:20), using the same kind of reversal Purim celebrates. The connection is thematic: the book does not predict Christ, and the fighting of chapter 9 is not a picture of his kingdom, which advances by suffering love. But Purim's pattern of remembrance, feasting, and generosity to the poor echoes in the Lord's Supper, where the church remembers the deliverance God has accomplished, and in the call to care for the needy.

hard.q: How should a reader understand the killing of 75,000 people in this chapter?
hard.a: This is the book's most difficult chapter for many modern readers. Several points are worth weighing. The Jews act under a royal decree permitting self-defense against those who would attack them on a day set for their annihilation; the text says they struck those who sought to harm them and those who hated them, not neutral neighbors. They refuse to take plunder, which the narrator stresses three times, suggesting they fought for survival rather than gain. Esther's request for a second day in Susa is harder to explain; some see it as eliminating continuing threats in the capital, others as excessive. Some scholars also read the book as a stylized story with large round numbers, not a precise report of casualties; others defend its historical character, noting that the ancient versions already give different figures. Christian readers have also noted that the Bible records many events without approving every detail, and that the New Testament forbids personal vengeance (Romans 12:19) while recognizing the state's role in restraining evil. Faithful readers differ on how much approval the narrator intends.

questions: The Jews refuse to take plunder though they are permitted to. What does restraint in the moment of victory reveal about a person or a community?
Purim was established so that later generations would remember. What practices help you remember what God has done in your life or your family's?
The feast includes gifts to the poor. Why might generosity to the needy belong naturally to the celebration of deliverance?
